utterances.text: After were you still in the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I then was transferred to the military police at the end of the year, at the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the town of Prijedor was attacked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And do you know when power was taken over in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A month later, that is, the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Which came first, the takeover of power or the attack on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. First power was taken over in April, and then there were incidents, and then on the 30th of May, Prijedor was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, I'm sorry for interrupting, but this is a clear case. We have heard a lot of evidence about the 30th of April and the 30th of May. Please go more directly to your questions. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question is linked to this date, and that is why I had to put the question to the witness once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So do you know where the headquarters of the command of the 43rd Motorised Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade at first was headquartered at Urije in Slavko Rodic Street and in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor, was the command moved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately, a couple of days after the attack, I don't know exactly how many days later, but anyway, it was shortly afterwards to Kozara Put, a company headquarters that is situated on the Banja Luka road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the command moved, were you also transferred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I joined a little earlier, maybe four or five or seven days earlier. I was deployed in security, to provide security for the move of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the investigation centres in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Your headquarters, after it moved, was it close to one of those investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Right across the road, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Which investigation centre was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Keraterm Investigation Centre, known as Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What was between the investigation centre and your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Banja Luka road, the main road, and there was a fence, a high fence made of wire netting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How far was the Keraterm compound from the headquarters of your command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was just across the main road, maybe 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was providing security of the command post, and later, I was posted as control at the entrance to the facility, as a porter who checked the persons entering, as a guard, a sentry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: While you were performing your guard duties, did you have a view of the Keraterm compound in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to identify persons walking around the Keraterm compound from your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: During your duty hours, were you able to see whether the Keraterm compound was lighted, was lit, at night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't very strong light because there were electricity restrictions, and the voltage was low. Sometimes there was no electricity in Prijedor for 20 days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: But was the compound lit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how your shifts were organised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had daily shifts of 12 hours, day shifts and night shifts. Because there were several of us, we took turns like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, did you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've known him from our early childhood, from primary school and secondary school, ever since then, to the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Upon your taking up your new duty, would you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where would you see him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him. He would come to the barracks compound where we were. He would come over for a cup of coffee. He would come inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately in time what time period you're talking about? Was this immediately after you came to the command post, to the new headquarters, or later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as we moved, immediately after that, ever since the beginning. No, actually, he inquired. He wanted to see what I was doing. There were no troops there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How did Zoran come to see you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He usually came on a small motorcycle. It's an automatic motorcycle, white in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did he spend some time at the entrance of the command compound or did he enter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he came in. He talked to us. He knew people inside, and he would talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In those days he was wearing normally a military uniform and he had something that we didn't have in those days, and that was a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you notice whether he had any bandage on him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was his left hand. I think it was his left hand, his left fist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When he came, did you personally talk to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, frequently. Either I spoke to him or he spoke to someone else and I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: On those occasions, did Zoran Zigic complain of pain in his hand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Of course he complained. He said it was bothering him when he was riding his motorbike and cleaning his rifle, but then we found it a bit strange because he was drinking at the same time and taking painkillers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran Zigic going to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to what he was doing in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, and judging from what he said, he was transporting food and water for those people who were detained there, who had been suspected of criminal offences, who had participated in the attack on Prijedor. There were some Serbs there, too, who were accused of theft or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In that time period, when you would see Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm compound, did you ever see him beating any one of the people held there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but he would usually make a lot of noise. That's what he was doing, yelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Until when -- or rather, until when did Zoran Zigic come to see you at your command headquarters? Or rather, could you tell us until what date you continued seeing him in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until about mid-June in 1992. Actually, he didn't come to see us either, because he was a boisterous sort of person and we were wondering where he was and why he wasn't coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you aware of the event that took place in Keraterm when a large number of people were killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 24th or -- to the 25th of the next month, that would be July, the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were you on duty at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, on the 24th, during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How long did your duty last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the morning until the evening. Well, not the evening, but until 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Tell us again, from how --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until -- from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening, a full 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what security was provided for the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: At the entrance -- the entrance of our command compound was opposite the entrance to Keraterm. And at the corner there was a ramp of some kind and a hut by the fence. And there was a sort of weighing machine of the Keraterm company and this hut there. That was the hut. There was a guard standing by the fence, parallel to our command, opposite, opposite the main road, the Banja Luka main road that is. One guard moved up and down that way, and I don't know what happened in depth, whether there were other guards further in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a technical problem with the transcript and interpretation, so I'm going to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Your duty shift, how long did it last, from when to when? Give us the time, please. When did your duty start and when did it end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening, or 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were the guards armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any machine-guns had been positioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was one by the weighing machine, to the right, to the right of the weighing machine and slightly forward, slightly in front of it, and there was a sort of barrier there, and that's where that machine-gun was. And then there was another one which was closer to us, that is to say, closer to our command, and it was on the left-hand side. It looked like a bunker of some kind which was where this second one was. Right by the grassy patch. I can't quite remember, but it was on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the weather was like that day, and I'm asking about the 24th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. It was very hot. The weather was very hot. It was a hot day and a nice sunny day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any detainees in Keraterm on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that it was a very hot day, so they were walking around in front of the halls, sitting down on the grass, grassy patch, some of them were inside because it was cooler, perhaps, inside. But they were walking around because it was very hot, and they were stripped to the waist. They had these water cans or something as well with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: On that particular day, do you remember whether the detainees received any food or any meals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were you at your guard post the whole day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was my duty to do that, to stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: On that day, did he come to your command compound, Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. We would notice him. That is to say, we would hear him, because as I say, he was noisy and boisterous, so we would have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you again, when did you hand over your shift? When were you replaced?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't stay exactly because we didn't keep it strictly to the minute, but in the evening at 1900 hours, that is to say, at 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already answered the question, but this is now the third time that Mr. Deretic has asked the question. Each time the witness has given the same response. I hope this will be the last time that the witness has to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: My next question is linked to your handing over your shift. Who took over the shift from you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague took over. His name was Zeljko Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Until you handed over your shift, on that particular day, did you see Zoran Zigic at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And I have two more questions for you, Witness. Before the war came to Prijedor, you said that you knew Zoran Zigic from earlier on. How long ago, how much time before the war broke out did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say about 25 years. I've known him for 25 years, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran frequently before the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said we went to school together. We went to the same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What was Zoran Zigic's hair colour then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The same as it is now, black, very black.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: While you saw him while you went around and before you came to the Kozara Putevi company, did you ever notice him that he had dyed hair at any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with earrings in his ears?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. Never. It wasn't his style.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see him ever wearing black gloves with the fingers cut off?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And lastly, can you describe briefly the kind of man Zoran was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The kind of man. Well, as a personality, I think he was a good friend. He's always been a good friend, and prior to the war -- I don't know what happened. As far as I was able to notice, during the war itself he drank a lot. I don't know what happened to him, but I think the war affects all of us, and people who never drank started drinking. People who never smoked started smoking. And I think he changed in the course of the war, that the alcohol, the drink changed him. I think that he should have gone for treatment for this condition. Had he done so, everything might have been different. As far as I can see now, and I'm very sorry to see that and to say it, that all the things that have been attributed to him were attributed because of the alcohol, because of the drink. And I think that even if he did something, he did something in the absence of his presence of mind because he wasn't sober.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I don't have any more questions for this witness, and I think we have kept within the time limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic. Thank you. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what were your duties in the 43rd Motorised Brigade from the 16th of September, 1991, until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end? My duties were, to begin with, at the beginning, to provide security for the command, the command post, and that means to stand guard, to do guard duty. I had no other special duties until the end of 1991. Later on, as I said, when the command post was transferred from the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks to the firm Kozara Putevi, a new headquarters, I once again provided security and I was posted at the entrance. I did guard duty at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why were you transferred to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why I was transferred? Well, let me tell you. I was in Western Slovenia to begin with, and then I had a pause, an intermission, because I had received an injury to my knee. I was ill. And then I was assigned a new post. Actually, that same year, in 1991, as we did not have military police in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks in Prijedor, it's a small barracks, this was established, and I was assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you on duty as a military policeman between the 23rd and 26th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 23rd, 26th, you say. May? I think I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was your duty or duty during those days, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. The 22nd of May? I think that -- May. You're asking me about May. I was in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, if you're talking about the 22nd of May. I was in the barracks then, the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, and I was the shift leader in there, in the barracks. And as a policeman, I had to distribute the policemen and the shifts within the barracks' compound. And there were about 50 guards at the time, and that was the assignment I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many guards were on your shift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks you mean, or Kozara Putevi company? Do you mean in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, in those first --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where it was located first, is that what you mean? I don't think we understood each other. Which location of the command are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the first location, how many guards were there -- can I finish my question, please. In the first location where you served as a military policeman and you were a shift leader of the guard shift, how many guards were on your shift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Usually, and that was standard practice at that time, to have about ten guards. But as between the takeover of power and the attack on the 30th of May, there were daily provocations. There were killings, attacks on the army by the extremists who took part in the attack on Prijedor. I was given the assignment of stepping up the guard in that particular barracks, of increasing the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So approximately when the guard -- the number of guards on your shift or in the barracks was stepped up, as you put it, how many guards eventually served on your shift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think there might have been about 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Fifty, all right. And as the guard shift leader, what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, normally, I would distribute them around. I would give them cautions as to if the barracks came under attack, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the guards on your shift look to you for instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the younger ones, more or less, yes, but of course, each guard received a piece of paper, document, compiled by the command that they had had to read through, instructions, containing instructions, which stipulated the conduct of the guards and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you were on duty at those barracks as the guard shift leader, would you give orders to the guards on your shift, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I would just distribute them. I gave them some instructions as to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would the guards on your shift follow your instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Zoran Zigic would come over for a cup of coffee to where you were on duty. I think now we are moving to the second place where you were on duty as a military policeman or as a guard. He would come over to those barracks where you were, across the road from Keraterm, from the Keraterm camp. Well, actually, I don't want to put words into your mouth.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where would Zoran Zigic come from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly from town, or sometimes he would be passing by, that is to say from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did he ever walk across the street, walk across the Banja Luka road from the Keraterm camp to where you were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He drove food and water, and of course he had to cross, that is to say to go in there, during that period of time when I saw him, up until the middle of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic simply walk across the road from the Keraterm camp to where you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He would just drop by with a motorcycle. I don't know which side he actually came from. Usually he would come on his motorcycle, moped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say that you spoke to him frequently during that period. How frequently?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I tell you? Perhaps a few days, in the course -- space of a few days, couple of times, every couple of days, and not only me. I said he would chat to me or some of the -- my other colleagues who were there. It didn't mean that he came specifically to talk to me. He would drop by. And he was noisy, he was boisterous, you would hear him talking. He would start shouting, and usually he was a bit tipsy. And even when he's not tipsy, he has the habit of speaking in a loud voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that Zoran Zigic complained about pain in his hand, that it bothered him as Mr. Zigic drove his motorcycle and as he cleaned his rifle. But Mr. Zigic was able to ride that motorcycle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, Mr. Zigic was able to clean his rifle and keep it clean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how far he kept it clean. I don't know what the maintenance level was, but probably he could. Of course you can hold it with your elbow, support it with your elbow as well, and he had the other four fingers of his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the 24th of July, when you were on duty at those barracks, between 7 a.m. and 1900 hours, did you see anybody at the Keraterm camp that you recognised, anybody that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I noticed some of the prisoners that I knew, I knew them by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You could see those prisoners, you could recognise them, from where you were across the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Besides the one machine-gun that you talked about during your direct testimony, did you ever see a second machine-gun set up at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Deretic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness stated loud and clear that he had seen two machine-guns and explained where each of them were located. Why does the -- my friend of the Prosecution ask about one now and whether there was another one? I'm not clear what he's trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, please proceed. I think that the question has been cleared up anyway, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm grateful for the clarification if I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were on duty that day from 7.00 in the morning until 1900 hours. Did you leave the Keraterm camp at 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. I went home for a rest. I went to my own house, home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How far is your home from the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's about three to four kilometres away, perhaps a little more, four to five kilometres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Hear anything unusual that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What could I hear if I was asleep?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Even if I did hear shooting, I didn't pay attention because there was shooting all the time. They would -- there would be gunfire all the time. It wasn't anything out of the ordinary, anything unusual. You would hear shooting, ten, five times during the day, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, was it usual to hear shooting coming from a place 30 metres away from barracks that you were guarding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear any shooting coming from the direction of the Keraterm camp that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have just told you that I was asleep at home that night, and the distance was four to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it's your testimony -- I'll explain why I'm asking this question. We have heard a lot of testimony that there was shooting, even intense shooting, for several hours that evening coming from the Keraterm camp. Even witnesses testifying on behalf of Mr. Zigic have testified to that. Is it your testimony that you heard no shooting that night?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what -- there was mention of what the Prosecutor is talking about now, but the witnesses did say that they were just 700 metres or a kilometre away from the shooting, but the witness has said that his own house is more than four kilometres away from the Keraterm compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, please proceed. The witness has already answered. He said he did not hear the shooting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Zoran Zigic was a good friend and you said that you've known him for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But that apparently he drank a lot during the war and he changed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic beat or abuse anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not, and let me tell you, I was present on one occasion, how shall I put it, in a cafe, in a coffee bar, a catering establishment, when he came in drunk, and I think he took out a pistol, and everybody fled, just perhaps a few people stayed on, because you never knew what he was going to do, what his reaction would be. So that was his behaviour. He was boisterous, he made a lot of noise. And people tended to avoid him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say everybody fled except for a few people when Mr. Zigic took out that pistol, just to be clear, is it -- to your knowledge, is it because some of the people there were afraid that Mr. Zigic might fire that pistol?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say he might fire. People just tended to steer clear of him when they saw he was drunk. They thought there might be a brawl of some kind. It needn't have been a shooting from a pistol, but that something would happen, an incident of some kind, some provocation or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that incident in the cafe happened, that you recall today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been sometime in mid-April, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What -- 1992. I know that because it was a bit cold and the cafe has tables outside, but the garden of the cafe was closed and it was inside. It was slightly cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What's the name of that cafe that you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it was in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The centre of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have the court's indulgence, please? Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Deretic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that your house was at least four kilometres away from Kozara Putevi company. Can you tell us exactly where your house was located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the road, on the Prijedor-Dubica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Between the Kozara Putevi company and your house, are there any hills? Are there any woodland?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and I was going to say that myself actually, because the noise is not the same. It doesn't travel the same way. People could throw a bomb and you wouldn't know which direction it was coming from, the explosion came from, because of the hills in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And one more question for you, Witness. You said you were in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were there any other people present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you know those people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the people in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Starting with the waiter, I think he was a Muslim. And then there were Serbs, there were women and men, adults. It was -- they were a mixture of ethnicities, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to know more and understand better about what you were saying about the attitude of Mr. Zigic. You said he was a good friend prior to the war, everything was all right, and but then during the war he drank a lot and changed, and you concluded that he should have gone for treatment. Of course, not everybody who drinks has to go for treatment. To your knowledge, in all this framework, what led you to this conclusion that should be a man for -- who was -- he should have been treated? In this instance of the cafe, you mentioned that people ran away, fled, because he could have been violent. Were there any expressions of violence that you know of when he was drunk?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me how I reached that conclusion. Well, that's my personal opinion. I think that he should have sought help, treatment for his drinking problem. But of course, it was a war. There was a war on, so you can't do that kind of thing during the war. The best thing is not to be where a war is happening. And I would say that any alcoholic ought to be treated, go for treatment, not only people who are aggressive, but who are docile and drunk as well. And as far as his aggressiveness is concerned, I think that that was because he lost consciousness when he was drunk. I think he even used some soft drugs. I don't know. I don't know about that, actually. But the way he looked like at certain times, I think that might have been the case, too. And that is not only my opinion, I heard others talk about that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So I can conclude that you considered him -- you considered that his aggressivity should have led to treatment, and that people, as you said, fled away from him for his aggressivity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness, just a few very brief questions. Were you yourself ever inside the Keraterm camp? Did you yourself ever go inside the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the description of my duties it says that I am not allowed to leave the facility which I am assigned to guard. And also, we were prohibited additionally from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's enough. My next question --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I never entered, to tell you quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You said that the camp -- I'm sorry, that the barracks that you were guarding, the headquarters you were guarding was across the road, across the Banja Luka road from the Keraterm camp. Can you tell me approximately how wide that road is? And just to put it in personal terms, is the Banja Luka road that separated the Keraterm camp from where you were doing your duty at the headquarters, was it, for instance, as wide as from where I am to you, or as wide as for where I am to the back of where the public gallery is? Or if you know in metre terms approximately, but just give me some notion of how wide that road is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the asphalt, the actual carriageway of the road?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, that's one part of it, yes. But if you want to answer it in terms of how far away from the point you were performing your guard duties to the actual places in the Keraterm camp where you said you could see people, which would be obviously farther away than the road itself, however you want to answer it. I just want to get some notion of the distances.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The main road itself in our country would be wide about six to eight metres, something like that. Then from their fence, the Keraterm fence to the fence of our compound where we were on guard, there would be under 30 metres. About 30 metres, 25 to 30 metres in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So your testimony, if I heard it correctly, is that across those approximately 30 metres you were able to recognise people who were walking around in the camp. That was your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And your testimony was also that you could, I believe, hear voices across the road and recognise Mr. Zigic's voice, because I know you testified that he tended to shout and to be more boisterous, perhaps louder than other people. But your testimony is that across those 30 metres you could hear him on occasion, or whenever you did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was the Banja Luka road well travelled? I mean, were there lots -- during the times you were on duty, was there trucks and cars going, or was it not well travelled by trucks and cars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't very busy because there was no fuel, no cigarettes, no electricity, no water, nothing, so it wasn't busy. Only when necessary did people drive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were there any other people besides Mr. Zigic that you could either recognise from your vantage point across the road, or recognise their voices?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Give me -- I don't want to know their names, but just give me an approximate number of the people, if you had to name their names, you could say that you recognised them both physically or if you recognised their voices from across the 30-metre distance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, how many people would you say, just approximately, that you did recognise, either physically or by voices, from across the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite a number, actually. But I don't know some of their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I don't want --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I do know the names of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm not asking you the names. So there were quite a few people. A couple of dozen or something like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: You talked about Mr. Zigic riding his motorcycle or moped. Can you tell me whether or not when he started up that motorcycle or moped it was very noisy, or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Noise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. When you said that he came, when he came to visit you at the barracks, sometimes you remembered him riding a small motorcycle. At one point you called it a moped. I'm just asking you, when he would start it up, as I assume he had to in order to leave the place, did it make much noise? That's all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you're familiar with the type of moped I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But it's not one that doesn't make any noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It doesn't make any noise. Okay. All right. I'm sorry, I'm not familiar with that, but that's exactly what I wanted to know, and thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a small motor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Small capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. To follow-up on that question, what could one hear better, Zigic's voice or the noise of the motor of the motorbike?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Zigic's voice. This motorcycle doesn't make any noise, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question, Witness Stojanovic. What was the visibility? You spoke of a fence between your vantage point. How high was that fence? How high was the fence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: roughly like that door, maybe even higher. About two metres and something, two and a half, maybe three. They're really high fences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How tall are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One metre 60, I think, or 70, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. One metre 70. And the fence was two and a half metres high?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two and a half, maybe three. I don't know exactly. It's a standard type of fence, factory-made, that existed there while the company was operating. These are standard fences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have no more questions, Witness. Thank you very much for coming and for answering our questions, and we wish you a safe journey to your place of residence. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise, if I may clear up this question that you have put to the witness. Would you be kind enough to ask the witness what kind of fence it was, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has already explained, but to make things quite clear I'm going to ask him. What type of fence was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said it is a fence -- you want me to explain it in detail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's probably about two by two, the panels, and in between there's netting. You're probably asking me because of the visibility, what kind of fence it was, because at that distance you don't even notice the wire mesh. You just notice the frame, because it -- these are squares of two-by-three millimetre wires, made of wire, so you can see everything, if that is your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Thank you very much for coming. I wish you a safe journey to your place of residence and success in your work. Will the usher see the witness out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and all the best to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic. I think that we now have Zeljko Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence for Mr. Zigic calls its 11th witness, that is, Zeljko Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gavranovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read the solemn declaration, please, that the usher has given you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Gavranovic, for coming. For the moment, you will be answering questions from Mr. Deretic, after that by the Prosecutor, and also the Judges. So Mr. Deretic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavranovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Will you please give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Gavranovic, son of Dragutin. I was born on the 19th of January, 1960, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I am a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: From when until when?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 16th of September, 1991, until the 15th of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In what unit did you serve during the war in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I served in the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a soldier, a Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were you later assigned to another duty?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned from the Slovenia theatre of war, I was assigned to a military police unit securing the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness. Could you approach the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor, where did you perform your duties?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor, I performed my duties at the Prijedor barracks, and later at the command post when the headquarters moved to the facilities of the Kozara Putevi Enterprise in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: During your shift duty, where were you on duty? What location?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I mostly was on duty at the entrance, at the porters, at the entrance to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were your duties organised in shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How long were your shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: We had 12-hour shifts during the day and during the night mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where was your position? Where was it located in the command?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to the compound of the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was one of the investigation centres in Prijedor close to your command post?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the Keraterm Investigation Centre. It was right across the Prijedor to Banja Luka main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In those days, did you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Since when had you known him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I've known Zigic Zoran for the past 25 years or so. When we were young, we were friends. We went out sometimes together, dancing, to dance halls. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After you were transferred together with your command to a new location, that is the premises of the Kozara Putevi company, did you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What was Zoran Zigic wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran mostly wore a military camouflage uniform with a red beret on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did he have any bandages on him in those days?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a visible bandage on his left hand, as he had had an accident. I really don't know what had happened, but anyway, his left hand was bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Zoran Zigic would come to -- inside the Kozara Putevi compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would drop in, in passing, but he would come to visit us when he had some free time because we had some friends in common, and he had some friends amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How did he come?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: He came on a small moped, an automatic motorcycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In that period, would you see Zoran entering the Keraterm Investigation Centre compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As he was a member of the reserve police force, I think, he was working on the delivery of food and water to the persons under investigation there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I pressed the wrong button.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you please judge the distance between your guard post and the fence of the Keraterm Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. From my guard post, about 25 to 30 metres was the distance to the Keraterm fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: From your guard post, did you have a view of the entire Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In those days, do you remember what the weather was like?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was summertime. We arrived there at the beginning of June, so it was sunny and fine all summer. It was very hot actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So what kind of visibility did you have of the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you work night shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In that time period, was the Keraterm compound lighted?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After your command moved to the Kozara Putevi facility, for how long a time period did you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but some 10 or 15 days. At first he would drop in more often, but later, I don't know why, he was dismissed from the reserve police force and he didn't come, and I heard that he had gone to the front lines with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranovic, in that time period, you said that you were on duty at night. Did you ever see Zoran Zigic at night in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Usually the Territorial Defence people came from -- for night security of the investigation centre. And during the daytime, it was mostly the policemen. And Zoran would come only when delivering food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the event when, in a single night, dozens of people were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on duty that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: From when until when were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I was on duty from 1900 hours until the next morning at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us roughly what the date or month of year that was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the end of July, I think. No. I know exactly. The night between the 24th and the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How is it that you remember that date with such precision?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe anyone who had experienced something like that would remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Who did you take over duty from that night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: From a military policeman called Dragan Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After you took over your shift, what was the situation like? Was anything unusual going on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, everything was regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, did you notice any changes within the Keraterm compound after you took over your shift?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no changes except that around 2100 hours, or maybe a little later, additional security forces arrived from the Territorial Defence. These were all elderly people who were not sent to the front. So members of the Territorial Defence came. These were elderly people who came only to provide security at the investigation centre because they would not be sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did that apply to that evening alone or was this a regular practice?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was customary. It happened every evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that these people arrived around 2100 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, around about then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you notice then any changes within the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular. They were distributed to take up guard posts, and it was only later, after 2200, that some disturbance started in the investigation centre, which had never occurred prior to that evening. There was commotion, so the guards told us that the prisoners were rebelling or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around 2200 hours, or maybe even later, we started hearing voices, some kind of Muslim prayers from inside and some songs in a language that I couldn't understand then or now, some kind of prayers, and these became louder and louder by the minute, and then there was banging and thumping. They broke the glass on the windows. They started tearing down the inventory, the beds, the pallets they were sleeping on. At least that is what I learned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you hear the soldiers who were providing security inside? Did you hear them communicate with the prisoners, talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, because they told us that something unusual was happening, so we too were on the alert with our weapons on the ready. And I saw from my position that two or three policemen who were providing security were going to the door of the hall where this was happening, and they were shouting at them through the closed doors to calm down, to be quiet, and that they would take steps if they continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: From this distance in time, could you be more precise about the time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean. The -- this disturbance or this unrest occurred around midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: But until then, was there any shooting? Were there any shots fired by the security personnel in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because there was an explicit order not to fire because intervention units of the police would come should anything occur. So there was a prohibition on shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how the Keraterm compound was secured?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There was physical security provided by the policemen and the Territorial Defence, the policemen on duty and Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Since you said that you were on duty at the entrance gate to the command post, that is the facilities of the former Kozara Putevi company, from your position, could you see any machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many machine-guns were positioned there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two, old models of machine-guns, of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was the Keraterm compound lighted that night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was lit every evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: On iron pillars. This was lighting used for industrial purposes, with white lights on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What happened after midnight?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since this disturbance within the hall where the detainees were held did not cease already around a half an hour after midnight, they started breaking down the door of the hall in which they were held, and they broke the aluminium panel on the bottom of the door, and they started coming out individually, disregarding the demands of the soldiers to halt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since two or three persons had already come out and didn't want to stop, they were running towards the neighbourhood of Cirkin Polje, the security guards, and I can say that with certainty, I heard them calling them to stop, but they paid no attention. And throughout this time the prayers inside continued with cries of Allah-u-ekber. For me, this was very upsetting because I didn't believe that they would try to flee from a secured compound, but they paid no attention, and the policemen were forced to open fire. First I believe they fired into the air, but that had no effect, and then they had to shoot at them to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: From the moment you took over your shift until the moment the shooting started, were you observing throughout what was happening in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment the commotion started, we, too, had to be on the alert and to get as close to the compound as we could, to the fences, and from there we could see very well what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Until that point in time, had you noticed Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: That evening? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: The shooting by the security guards of Keraterm, how long did it last? And what was the intensity of the firing, was it the usual, standard type of shooting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I saw that the detainees, more and more of them were trying to escape and go through that door. To begin with, the shooting was more intensive to stop the people escaping, and it went on for quite some time. It might have been until 3.00 to 3.30 a.m, and then there was a lull, and it was more sporadic until the escape had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in the Keraterm compound that evening, whether it was more lighted at one point during the night than usual, the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after an hour and a half or two hours when the shooting had reached its peak, at that time the policemen brought in a new reserve flashlight which they positioned at the -- towards the edge of the compound to be able to control the halls and the door of the place where the detainees were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that you were on your shift -- or would you like to repeat, when were you doing this shift? When did you hand over your shift, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I handed over my shift at 7 a.m., in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Before handing over your shift, did you in the Keraterm camp see a Schlepper truck of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning a yellow Schlepper truck turned up to the compound. I know that for sure because I know that the AutoTransport company of Prijedor had this particular type of yellow trailer truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where did the trailer truck arrive at, what location, what spot?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was brought to in front of the building that the detainees were escaping from, the detainees who died that night, and it was parked in reserve. Its back side was facing the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the trailer truck was used for?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because I saw people, some of the detainees, two or three of them, perhaps, they were loading up the people who had been killed up onto the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of those individuals, I mean the people that were loading the dead bodies up onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise anybody, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognised Zlatan Zeric, and I know him because we called him Arso, the popular one, or Aco. We referred to him as Aco. That was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long it took for these bodies to be loaded up onto the trailer truck? Let me ask more specifically: Were they loading it up until you took over -- handed over your shift?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before I left, the trucks were loaded, and then some people were called out from the rooms where the detainees were, and they were told to wash down the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You said that you left at 7 a.m. from the Keraterm compound. Up until that time, did you see Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was not in the Keraterm compound. I did not say that. I was in the Kozara Putevi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I misspoke. I stand corrected, my mistake. What I wanted to say was, from your guard post until you left your shift, handed over your shift, did you see Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: That evening when you took over your duties until you left your shift, handed over your shift, did you see Zoran Zigic at all in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did he come to the Kozara Putevi facility at any time during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know or did you learn the next day after the events whether there were any rumours going round town, the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People learnt what had happened that night. They were talking about it. Everybody knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And my last question: You said that you have known Zoran Zigic for a long time. Could you describe him as a person? What kind of person was he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Zoran was -- how can I put it? He was -- had a lively temperament. He was temperamental. He would drink from time to time, but he was more temperamental than the rest of us. But generally, he was okay. For those of us who knew him, he was good to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: I have an additional question. Could you distinguish in time, before the war and during the war, can you make a distinction between the two; that is to say, looking at him during these two periods, was there a difference in his behaviour when it came to alcohol and drinking?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war he was a taxi driver, and so he drank less frequently. But as far as I was able to see during the war, he was under the influence of drink more often than he was before. When he was off work before, he would have a drink and get a bit tipsy, go and have a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions. The Defence did wish to show some diagrams, but in view of the time that we have at our disposal, we refrain from presenting that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Deretic. You took up half an hour. I think that before we have the cross-examination, we shall take our break for lunch, and I think that would be convenient at this point. But before we adjourn, I'm going to ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. As we said, we are now going to adjourn for 40 minutes, so we'll leave that safety net of 10 minutes and have a 40-minute recess. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Let us resume. Witness, you will now answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, I will go straight to the time that you served or worked in the Kozara Putevi location. How many people were on duty with you during a shift?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: More or less four or five took turns at the location where I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about a specific post or position at the entrance; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So during a 12-hour shift, there were four to five people who kept on changing; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. One would be on duty, and after 12 hours, a replacement would come. There was one resting always and one working most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were standing at the entrance 12 hours continuously?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't standing. We could sit down. We could walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Within 12 hours, did anyone replace you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: If it should be necessary, if we went for lunch or to the toilet, then this reserve person would stand in for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So it's correct that sometimes you will be not there at the entrance, right throughout the 12 hours that you served?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Altogether in the compound, in the Kozara Putevi location, how many guards were there at a given time during a 12-hour shift?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to us, from the military police providing security for the command post, and the commander, there was also the military who didn't go to the front line. There were five or six guard posts. They had a different regime of shifts so they changed every three hours or so. So I don't know exactly how many soldiers there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you all have -- when you call it a barracks, did you all have soldiers almost 24 hours in that location in this barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a barracks in the strict sense. It was just the command post of our brigade. The barracks was situated elsewhere, in another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who was the commander during the month of --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was Colonel Arsic, Vladimir Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, think very clearly. Was there a curfew in force during that time, which exempted the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: A curfew did exist but the soldiers were not exempted, because during the curfew, no one was allowed to move around without a special permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Just to make whether -- see whether I am clear. You said in your direct examination the distance from the place that you were -- where you stood guard and to the fence of the Keraterm camp was 30 metres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: More or less. I don't know exactly. It may have been a metre or so more, but about 30 metres up to the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then from the fence within that Keraterm camp there was this grassy area, then the road, then again the grassy area. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: From the place where the detainees were held and the compound that they moved in, yes, there was grass, fence, road. So the distance may have been up to 30, 40, or even 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you're talking over from the rooms to the fence in the camp there's about another 30 to 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you ever gone to the Keraterm camp, inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I did enter on a couple of occasions. I had some acquaintances there who were detained during the war operations, so I would take them cigarettes, or their wives would bring some food for them and then I would take it in to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: While you were on duty in the night, did you see detainees walking around during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not during the night. At night they were locked up in the hangar or, rather, inside the premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know as to how many rooms were there where the detainees were kept in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Four. Three, and the fourth mainly held Serb soldiers and prisoners who had avoided their military obligation, and later on that room was not used, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen during this time that you were in the Kozara Putevi, or even the time that you visited the camp, have you seen the condition of the prisoners, their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them. I don't know what exactly you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were they beaten --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: They were in a normal condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see injuries? Did you see them being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During the night, did you hear cries or moans coming from the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During the day, have you seen prisoners being brought out in front of the rooms and being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them being beaten. When they were taken in for interrogation, they were taken to a room inside where the interrogators were, and I don't know how they treated them inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, now, you said that you were on duty on the night of the 24th of July. After you took your post at the entrance, did you see anything unusual in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You didn't hear any singing, you didn't hear any noises coming from the Keraterm camp until the time that you said you heard noise?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
