utterances.text: Yes, the way I told you. Around 21 or 2200 hours, I don't know exactly, that is when the commotion started, the noise, the breaking of furniture inside and other inventory. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you heard --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: That's when they started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you hear that breaking of furniture, or is it what you heard from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard this breaking of things. The glass on windows was broken, the thumping on the steel door. You can hear that well, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't know as to whether the prisoners were given food during that day?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they did, but I assume that they did because they received food every day regularly from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You don't know as to whether they were let out that day from the room?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I wasn't in the day shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw and heard -- you saw the soldiers in the camp telling the detainees not to create trouble. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And then some shots were fired in the air, then after that some people escaped and they were shot. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you see --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Not like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you. I said that since the prisoners did not want to stop the disturbances inside, the policemen warned them to stop, but they didn't stop until maybe half an hour after midnight when they broke down the lower panel of the door in which they were held and when they started coming out. And upon the cries of the policemen that they should halt, the normal military term, "Stop or I'll shoot," they didn't stop. And then a couple of shots may have been fired into the air, upon which they pay no attention again, and then the policemen had to stop them because they were fleeing towards an inhabited part of town called Cirkin Polje, so it was to be expected that in the fury, in that condition, they may have -- they could have been capable of committing some evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: These prisoners were, according to your knowledge, were not armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know even later that there were some prisoners shot inside the room?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see at any time -- you spoke about a machine-gun. Did you see the machine-gun being fired?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: One machine-gun was fired when the situation climaxed, when there was the largest crowd rushing to the door, then they opened fire from the machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said the shooting went on until 3 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that people -- now, did you observe -- sorry, I will rephrase. Did you know as to from which room these prisoners, as you say, attempted to escape?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know, because I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which room is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You say that the shooting went on from 12.30 onwards until 3.00 in the morning. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: More or less, maybe until 3.00, maybe until half past 3.00, but something like that. At first it was of higher intensity. Then it subsided gradually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said there was high intensity and subsequently there were, you know, subsequent shooting. Why was that? Why was that? Why was that shooting being done?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There was shooting because the detainees wanted at all cost to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is that even after the prisoners had seen that, the early ones being shot and being killed, still everybody gradually, during intervals, that they tried to escape? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally was astounded. It was fanatical, in my opinion, for people to try to escape when they didn't stand a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw the bodies in the morning -- in the morning, the bodies being loaded into a truck. And you said you recognised a person, Aco; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: We called him Aco, but his real name is Zlatan Zeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you know -- did you see as to what happened to the wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see what happened to them, but probably afterwards -- we didn't hear anyone else coming so they were probably treated in hospital in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any of the wounded being loaded into the truck, now that you have seen the dead bodies being loaded?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that. I saw people; I didn't see whether they were wounded or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you get to know -- you said that because you got to know that the prisoners had broken the furniture subsequently and the beds and so on. Did you know as to how many prisoners, detainees, were killed in that massacre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I heard there were between 60 and 80 people, but I really can't say myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: As it's not still clear with regard to the three-hour period of shooting, could you explain, did it take the people who were present in the compound of the Keraterm camp to shoot for three hours to stop this escape?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't intensive shooting that went on for three hours, but as some of the detainees tried to escape, the policemen would open fire, the guards would open fire. It wasn't a constant -- a constant gunfire, intensive gunfire, for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before this intensive shooting or even the escape, did you at any time see a perimeter being formed or -- to prevent the people from getting away, some precautionary action being taken by the guards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't any special barrier there or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that there was an Intervention Platoon that came, which reinforced -- to assist the Territorial Defence personnel who were there. Did you see any of those people? Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the reserve force of the Territorial Defence came, and they were elderly people, people who were not of military age and capable of going to the front. So they would come every night to provide night-time security, additional night-time security, to the investigation centre. I didn't know them because most of the people were older than me, and I didn't see them around town, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gavranovic, just another matter. Before this Intervention Platoon came, as to how many -- did you see as to how many people, how many guards, were there in the Keraterm camp in that night? Because it is a normal, usual night.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the usual number, up to ten. I don't know exactly but about ten. And the situation was regular, standard, not more, not less, the number that was usually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then, what reinforcements were brought in?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: During the day, there was no need for reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have interrupted. I'm asking about after the, you know, the help was -- assistance was called. You said that the intervention platoon came in. As to how many personnel came there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't an intervention platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness, Your Honour, has just given an answer. I was going to object and say that the witness did not mention an intervention platoon at all, at any point, but the witness himself has answered. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic, that is quite true. But let me reiterate, the witness is there. He is there to answer, so you don't have to protect your witnesses so much. I apologise for that comment. I apologise for that comment. It was just a comment, but as I say, the witness is fully capable of answering for himself. Please proceed, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, when you -- correct me if I'm wrong. Did any other personnel come out -- come into the camp after the trouble started in support of the guards who were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, except that platoon which was designed for additional security to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, could you clear up this position a little bit because your direct examination is somewhat different, as I see it. Could you say now even your last answer, "Except that platoon which was designed for additional security to the camp," what was this additional security that day which was there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was just during the night shifts when there was a higher degree of caution, and then they would have some -- the platoon that came, they would take up their guard posts along the Keraterm compound, the perimeter of the Keraterm compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see a police or any other vehicle come during the night to the Keraterm compound during the fateful night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I can't say for sure. I can't say I saw any vehicle come for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- are you taking note of the time? Are you controlling it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm always aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were given orders not to use your weapons, is that correct, or shoot during that night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: We weren't providing security for the camp. We had nothing to do with that, so we didn't have any instructions to fire at the camp, nor was there any need to. We were security for the command post, so that was our -- all our duty was, to provide security and to defend and protect the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the guards in the Keraterm camp, the people who were securing that area, they were not precluded or prevented from using their weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the guards in the camp probably had their own instructions to ensure the security of both the detainees and the camp, to prevent the detainees from trying to escape. What their orders actually were, I really can't say, but I assume that that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, during a situation as what you explained in your direct examination, and even under the cross-examination, is it your position that you were not permitted to fire or use your weapons in a situation as such?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In the situation I personally was, no, I was not allowed to fire towards the detainees, the prisoners, and we didn't do that. We did not have permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, to conclude, you're a person, according to you, who was on duty outside, the closest to the Keraterm camp in the barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. But outside the Keraterm compound, across the road, and then you get to the Kozara Putevi company's compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you saw and heard, according to you, the commotion and the trouble which has taken place in Keraterm camp, did you take any steps to inform any other person in the barracks or to ask for help? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: We were not in a position to ask for assistance, and the duty officer who was on duty that night, he saw everything from the command post, and he probably informed -- and probably he informed from Keraterm, from the police. He was informed by the police, probably, because the information went to the police station first, and then it was probably -- they probably informed the officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you being the person who was at the, you know, closest, you're unaware as to whether your command from the place that you were stationed that night, whether there was any request for assistance or any -- asking for any help?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you didn't inform anybody about this position. You simply think that it would have been -- that your senior officer or duty officer would have asked for help. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer was informed by us and by the police within the Keraterm compound, but what his competences and authorisations were after that, I don't know. Whether he asked or not, I don't know. That was at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes my ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Deretic for the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavranovic, you said that the detainees escaped in the direction of Cirkin Polje. Is that opposite to your command post?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Had they started escaping towards you and crossed the fence, would you have fired?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have one more question, but could we go into private session for a few moments?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After you heard, after you heard this commotion in Keraterm --

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, not yet, not yet. My next question will need private session, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After you heard the commotion there, did you remain by the hut that you were armed guard at, or did you move closer to the road towards the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I heard some out-of-the-ordinary occurrences going on there, I got out and moved closer towards the road so that if there were an attack on us, that I should be closer to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How many metres was it from your guard hut to the place you stopped at?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was it closer to Keraterm or further away from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was still further away from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So from the guard post to the road, that distance, this 20-metre distance, is it closer or farther from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. The witness had given a clear answer: "It was still further away from Keraterm."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put that question again and I'll be more precise this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: When you heard the commotion in Keraterm, did you yourself at the hut where your guard post was, did you approach the road, go up closer to the road towards Keraterm or did you go off further?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I went closer up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How much closer did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty metres closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have two more questions for private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Please proceed, judge. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. When you were asked if you have seen Mr. Zigic in the camp during that -- the night of the shooting, you said that from the moment you handed over -- you started your shift until the end, you did not notice Mr. Zigic in the camp. Now -- and then you mentioned there was a lot of commotion and a very chaotic situation. Could you with certainty affirm that, in such a situation, you could discover if someone was not there in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could say with certainty that I did not see Zoran Zigic because I know him, and by his gestures and his face and -- I would know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Despite all this running around and shooting and chaos, you saw everything that was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw everything. It wasn't the policemen and soldiers and Territorial Defence people running around. They had no need to run around. They were standing by the side and getting control of the situation. The running around was done by the prisoners who were trying to escape. And I guarantee that I did not see Zigic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So what were the other guards doing exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The other guards were standing at their guard posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Standing doing what?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were shooting were shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, since you had such a clear vision, you said that you couldn't, of course, see what was happening to the detainees inside the interrogation rooms, but when they were brought out and taken back to the rooms, could you see them, see if they were carried, if they were hurt, if they were walking steady?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was very rarely that I saw the prisoners at all, when they would be taken to interrogation and back. That's when I might see them. But all of them would return normally. Nobody carried them. They walked on their own two feet, normally. I don't know what the treatment they had -- they were given during the interrogation, I don't know that, but generally they were walking on their own, able to walk on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, concerning the escaping of the prisoners and the fact that they were -- they didn't stop even being shot, you said that the shooting was justified by the fact that they could have committed some evil going towards Cirkin Polje, and then you said that they were not armed. What -- and then you said even though -- you were asked if you would have shot them yourself, you said yes. Why would you have shot them if they were not armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in case they had crossed the road and were to attack me from any side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you have shot them --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably to protect me and the command post. Probably not because I'm not that kind of person personally. I myself am not. I'm not somebody who can shoot another man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you consider unarmed men would be dangerous enough to be killed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you should shoot an unarmed man, but he ought to be incapacitated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But then you yourself wondered very much, you said they wouldn't stop even -- they continued escaping even though they knew that they are being shot. Now, in your opinion, how -- why did they prefer being shot than surrendering?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I never thought about it along those lines. I really don't know why they didn't want to stop and why they acted as they did. I can't actually say myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And doesn't that mean that the person is completely desperate and has no escape?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is that everybody who left the investigation centre, almost everybody left normally. I don't know whether they had another way out or not. The impression that I gained, with the prayers and the singing that -- the chanting that was going on seemed to be a sort of fanaticism, so I don't know the way they thought there, what was in their heads. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have a few brief questions for you. As I understand your testimony, you stayed at your post all that night. I mean maybe except for possibly going to the bathroom or something like that, but you were there for your whole shift, is that right, from 7.00 to 7.00 at the guard post?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did I also understand you correctly that the disturbances, the singing, the thumping, the glass breaking, that sort of thing began around 10.00? Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately, 9.30, 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Around that time. Okay. How long was it between the time that that began, the disturbances began, and the first shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, it might have begun -- the detainees might have started escaping at about 12.30, which is when the shooting began, about half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it was about two to two and a half hours between the time that you first heard the singing, the thumping, that sort of thing, and the time you heard or saw shots being fired? That's right, isn't it? About two? Okay. Now, you talked about the -- finally the aluminum panel in the door being knocked out of the door and the people actually running out the door and fleeing. Now, you were standing at your post the whole night, as I understand, except you moved closer to the road at one point when the disturbances began. What's your estimate of how many detainees you actually saw come out the door?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, what's almost -- a number, a number, if you would.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume, and I heard, that there were between 60 and 80. I don't know the exact number, but most of them I saw escaping, and that's for sure. I saw that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You see, the problem is, "most of them" means there was some unknown number in the room. I don't know and you haven't testified as to -- maybe you probably don't know how many were actually in the room, so it's hard to say what "most of them" -- that's what I'm trying -- and we know later how many dead bodies you heard [sic], but I'm trying to get an answer that's in the middle there. You were standing at your guard post or near the fence for the entire time that this took place. I'm just asking you how many you personally saw run out the door. An estimate. I know you can't give me precise, an estimate.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Judge, I didn't say that I saw most of the people who were in the room and then went out. I saw most of the people who were actually trying to escape and saw them fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I myself don't know the number of people in the room, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand that. So again, we're just back to how many people estimated you saw come out the door?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Up to 50, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I was just looking for a number. Now, my second question would be, did you see the guards fire only as people emerged from the door, or at any time did you see them fire into the room from which the prisoners were coming? In other words, did the guards who were outside wait until the detainees were coming through the door and fire at them as they tried to run away, or did you see them fire into the room?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards fired just at those people who had come outside and tried to escape in the direction of -- and the time when nobody was coming out, they weren't shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So therefore, based on your observations, you would not be able to either testify to or even explain if other people testified to the fact that bullets, bullet holes were found inside the room. Based on your observation, you wouldn't have any explanation for that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. All right, all right. Now, again, in terms of how many approximately, by the end of the shooting in the area of 3.00 or 3.30, how many bodies would you estimate you saw, not heard about the next morning but that you saw out around the compound as having been shot and lying on the ground, shot or wounded or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say for certain how many there were, but it was a heap of people who were killed in their escape. I couldn't -- I didn't -- I wasn't able to count. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. My last question: You talked a little bit about the next morning and before you left your shift, before 7.00, and that I think you testified that you saw the truck come and the bodies being loaded onto the truck. And I think you answered a question that you were not able to tell from your vantage point whether everybody that was loaded on was killed, or maybe whether some were wounded. So my question to you would be: Up to the time that you left your shift, apart from that truck which you saw them loading bodies onto, did you see any other vehicles such as either ambulances or police cars or any other vehicles into which bodies were loaded, or only the one truck?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was watching, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: While you were watching, you just saw the one truck; is that what you're saying? In the morning.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was early morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what happened later on, what the activities were later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. But as you left, as you left at 7.00, you said by the time you left the truck had already gone, I think, is that right, or had driven away? Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were there any bodies left lying around on the ground after the truck was driven away?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Mr. Gavranovic, I have a few questions, too. How many days or shifts or time did you spend at this guard post before this night of the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was on duty there virtually from the beginning of June for as long as it was necessary. Maybe it was September or October that I was transferred from that guard post to provide security at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were there from the beginning of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at the time, did you have regular guard duty there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. When did you see the machine-guns for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The machine-guns were positioned there as soon as the investigation centre was established. I don't know the exact date. I know they were there, but probably immediately after the investigation centre was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let me reformulate that question. When you arrived to take up your guard duties there, were the machine-guns already there, or did they come after you had already started working there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Those machine-guns were always there on the ready. I can't tell you with certainty whether they were there when I arrived or after that because I didn't enter the compound, you see, so I didn't really register all those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But from your guard post, were you able to see the machine-guns or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question is, when did you see them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of June, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you took up your duties there, they were already there, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Another question for you: Could you regularly see the Keraterm compound? In other words, the position that you held, did it give you a view of the whole compound, or did you look there only if there was something out of the ordinary going on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: From where I stood, I was able to see the compound of the Keraterm, but if something unusual happened or when new detainees were being brought in, we paid more attention to see whether there were any acquaintances among them. But most of the time we could see what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that night you didn't see Zigic in the camp. Was there any one time when you did see Zigic in the camp, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: That night I didn't see Zigic in the camp, I'm quite certain of that, because madam asked whether there were any other vehicles in addition to the truck, and I would have noticed if he had come on his motorcycle or in the small van, so I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But except for that, the question is that you are certain that that night you didn't see Zigic. My question is, are you sure that on no other day or night did you see Zigic in the camp, on any one particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I would see him, yes. I saw him a number of times in the camp. That's quite clear, because I saw him driving in the food, when he came informally, and so on. I saw him on one occasion when Car -- now, what was his name? -- Jusufagic, when they brought him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What made you look or register the presence of Mr. Zigic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular to focus on him, but he was one of the few that I knew among those who were active in the camp, so I probably noticed him more than the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have no more questions, Witness, and thank you very much for having come. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to turn this into a rule, this must be an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But linked to your question when he saw Zigic for the last time, could we hear the witness answer that question, before the events in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't need that question. I'm sorry. Anyway, usher, you may accompany the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we now have a little time remaining to deal with a few questions, and they are rather urgent. I think the three topics that we have to address is protective measures for a witness for the Defence of Mr. Zigic, the question of a video conference for a witness for Mr. Prcac, and the translation - I fear to pronounce the word -- the word is razvodnik straze and sef smjene, these two terms. I'm sure you know what these mean. So perhaps we can take the three together. In view of the limited time at our disposal, I don't know whether there is anything else that is urgent that we have to address. I think not. But we do have to deal with these matters as quickly as possible. So the first question: Protective measures for Defence witness for Mr. Zigic. My question is to Mr. Stojanovic or Mr. Deretic. What protective measures are you requesting, and what are the grounds for that request? Is the question clear? I expect a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, very clear. I don't think there is any need for a private session because these are videolink witnesses under number 3 and 5. If you have the list in front of you, if I were to utter their names, we would have to go into private sessions. These were persons who were suspects before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecution also has the name, so we don't have to name them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps it may be an unusual request for safe conduct, as they are testifying in a country whose citizens they are and where they are residing, but I can only convey that entry to a building of an international organisation appears to them to be rather like an arrest. I hope that I will be able to persuade them, especially my friend Mr. Deretic who has greater authority, that that is not so. But personally, I am not quite familiar with video conferencing as a technique, but as far as I know, the public can see the witness and recognise his identity. If, in the Chamber's opinion, there is no need for safe conduct, we feel that a minimum protection would be to protect the identity of those witnesses, and that would be a pseudonym and facial and voice distortion. That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you haven't answered my question. What are the reasons? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I have already spoken about the reasons. These are persons who -- you know that they were on two indictments of this Tribunal, but the persons will be testifying about very concrete events. I assume that they may also name some persons who are their compatriots from the same town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, the translation I got, they appear on indictments or used to be on an indictment? Please don't look at the English. I got the French translation. The French translation told me that they appear on an indictment. So my question is: Is that the present or the past you're talking about? Which tense?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. As far as I can recollect, Ms. Arbour, who was the Chief Prosecutor, said that she was withdrawing the indictment but she's not excluding the possibility of them being indicted later on, not because there was a lack of evidence but rather because she was focusing on prosecuting people of a higher level, of a higher rank. So in a sense, they are still suspect and that is the reason for their fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me make a tour of the Defence regarding all these questions and then I'll give the floor to Ms. Somers. So let me now ask Mr. Jovan Simic. Let me hear your reaction to this question. What is the estimated duration for your video conference witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 30 minutes on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Jovan Simic. I think I can now give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers, as the third question is one that we can deal with separately perhaps. So Ms. Susan Somers, in any event, I would like to hear the reaction of the Prosecution, if you wish to react. Do you think -- don't you think that people who had been indicted and who have been removed from indictments are maybe more protected than people who never learned -- don't know whether they are indicted or not? I don't know, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that particular issue is not relevant right now for purposes of the safe -- the notion of safe conduct. The individuals who are the subject of this are -- I think are already getting an extreme gift from the Chamber, in that the Tadic decision on videolink suggests that videolink is not a preferred method of hearing, that in fact safe conduct would be the best method. This Chamber has been more than fair in permitting persons whose only basis for not coming to the Hague, which is the method that has been held to be preferred for all purposes, for testifying, absent extremely important circumstances, in the interests of justice, and I hardly think that the interests of justice were necessarily the basis for this motion by the Defence. There is no support whatsoever for adding safe conduct to an already-granted videolink, particularly in the territory of the RS, which territory has protected people from effectively coming to us on most occasions. So there is no legal ground whatsoever. The jurisprudence of this institution would not support it. And the notion that a person walks into a place on the territory of the RS, assuming that person is walking around freely anyway, with full identity known, there is no basis for suggesting any different set of circumstances upon walking into the location that has been selected for this particular videolink. The Prosecution firmly opposes any additional measures. I do not even see the basis, quite frankly, for any type of pseudonym or any other form of measure. These individuals are living in a protected status and have always been so living. It is absurd to suggest that if they walk back out to places where they have been walking and living freely since the war, that anything will happen to them. And I have seen no ground enunciated by anyone from the Defence that would change this picture. Therefore, I think that it would be a true mockery of the process to allow anything more than this Chamber has already very generously allowed. We would oppose, as I say. It would just -- I'll stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As far as the safe conduct is concerned, it's very clear what you said, but do you think that a witness in general, if he feels more safer - I mean his name is not known or face not seen - he might give us more information, even in your interest, in the interests of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think so in this instance because what is at issue is the walking into a building, from what I understand. The amount of information given seems not to be related to the safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm not talking safe conduct. I agree with you on safe conduct. But the fact that he can speak freely, don't you think that you, the Prosecution, can also be interested in finding out more from him? He might refrain from saying things if he especially is a witness of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may be very specific to these two individuals, my answer, for reasons which may become known during the course of examination, is no, I do not think it will make any difference whatsoever. And I -- again, in the course of examination, it will become clearer but, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Leave safe conduct aside for the moment. Do you have strong objections to, say, simply a pseudonym? I mean, the number of Prosecution witnesses that we have had who were given pseudonyms, even though they lived in a territory where they walked around like anyone else, has been fairly broad in this case, as well as in other cases, and I'm wondering how strong your objection is to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of those individuals had at one point been victims, although walking around freely in the territory, particularly, let's say, in Prijedor. This is a distinguishable situation. These people have never been in that category and, in fact, have enjoyed the full support of those in whose territory they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But times change and we have had situations where people who are on the -- certainly in other cases, not on this case so much, who were members of the VRS or something else, who were given closed session, protective conditions, et cetera, on the notion that, you know, people have -- even if you're in the territory which is currently under the control of the people that you used to belong to or that you belong to, that doesn't rule out possibilities of harassment, intimidation. I don't think the victim/not victim category is always an absolute rule. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I think one point that is distinguishable also is that they are testifying on behalf of the Defence in his territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You don't want to pursue that one. If you're on the Defence, you don't get protective measures, but if you're on the Prosecution, you do?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's not the suggestion, Your Honour. The territory issue is -- it is the territory of the individual affected. I don't see in this circumstance -- again, this matter, I'm sure -- I want to register our objection. However, it has to be in the Chamber's hands. I know it has been granted before. I have been involved in videolink situations where it has. I do not see this situation as one that would merit it. It is in the Chamber's hands with our recorded objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll just pursue my question. You mentioned that it will not be beneficial to you. You may not draw any interest in having them, in having a pseudonym or facial distortion, because I told you they might speak more freely. But what -- is there any -- does this put you in any disadvantage if they have pseudonym or facial distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the limitation of perhaps being able to discuss testimony would limit -- would be disadvantageous to us, but again, Your Honour, I want to make it clear I'm talking about these two individuals, and there are very specific reasons at least as to one and I believe it will spill over as to the other. Our limitations -- our hands are always tied to a certain degree in terms of pursuing other areas of information, but I do want to make clear that I know this has not been an outlawed practice in videolink and I know it has been applied judiciously. Therefore, I think I have to limit my comment to these particular individuals. I do not think it will be of any assistance to the Prosecution certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It will put you to a disadvantage?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It will not help us to have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It will not help you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, to respond, but I would like to add this. Would it be a problem for you to bring these witnesses here to the courtroom if they were granted safe conduct? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, certainly. I think that possibility is excluded in the case of this witness -- these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is it excluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that those persons were quite categorical regarding their refusal to come here, but they know what we are going to ask them. We told them that we would ask them about many things of which they had been charged and accused. They are ready to respond to such questions as well. Of course, all related to the charges against Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If these individuals do not wish to come here and testify, given safe conduct, which means given maximum protection that anyone can give them, I'm wondering what are the reasons why they're refusing to come here while accepting a video conference? I'm wondering why. I have a lot of difficulty in understanding that, because after all, safe conduct is the greatest guarantee that they can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it must be clear to you and me, of course, that that is so, but these are persons who were indicted and who have a high dose of doubt that they might be arrested again. And they know that they will be asked about matters that they have been charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never, Mr. Stojanovic. There must be a misunderstanding. Even if they are indicted, if they have safe conduct, the Prosecutor cannot arrest them. It is not possible, Mr. Stojanovic. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's no need for me -- for you to explain these things to me. I have every trust in your protective measures, but I am simply not capable of persuading them otherwise. The Defence will be questioning them about facts that are part of their own charges. And I even think, or that is, at least, my impression, that they will be quite truthful and sincere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you think that with a pseudonym and facial and voice distortion, they are available for testimony? They're ready to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, Your Honour, through a videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us how they see these protective measures, what their understanding of them is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, it is encouraging for them. After all, they will be staying within the territory of their own country, and I think that is acceptable for them. At least, I can guarantee for one of the two and that he will testify without any fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But having told us all that, I'm wondering why they don't testify in their own country, in their own territory, in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I told you that they were ready to mention the names of certain persons who are their compatriots from the same town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we will have a private session for a few minutes and then go back into public. That's what we have been doing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Just a moment to confer with my colleague, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the dilemma you are setting before us is quite understandable as far as I am concerned, but I must also try and put myself in their position and their attitude towards their testimony. They really do insist on this. And if you don't accept, but I do hope that you will grant our request, if you don't grant it, we will do our best to persuade them to attend a videolink in that way. I really cannot tell to what extent that videolink will be public for the citizens of Prijedor where they come from. They would not like that to be public for their co-citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are several issues here. A video conference, I think, it's not up to me to explain these things to you now, Mr. Stojanovic, but as you know, as we have done today, we can have a part in public which everyone can see, and there is a part that is in private which is not seen here in the public gallery, nor anywhere else. So I think that if names are being mentioned, then we go into private session, and in that way, we provide the protection the people need. The only thing is for you to be able to organise your examination in such a way as to put all the questions that you need to put in private session together, and then after that, the other questions in public session. So I think that's very easy, and that has nothing to do with the facial distortion, the voice distortion, because, you know, we're making an exception, but only when that is justified. We cannot do that so easily and lightly. There must be reasons. There must be exceptional circumstances to make an exception. As you know, the Chamber is ready to do that when that is necessary. So my suggestion to you would be that we have the video conference. As you know, we will be here in the courtroom. We will see the people on our monitors, and there will be a moment when we will say we're going into private session, and then you put those particular questions to the witness. And you explain this, you should explain this to the witnesses that they can be quite at rest, and then we will see how we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it is a fair proposal, but may I just add that we would ask for a private session even when we expect these witnesses to say things that are self-incriminating, not only when they mention names. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can talk about that. We can discuss it when the time comes. We can't anticipate the testimony now. So what we can say is that there may be reasons when we go into private session. We will grant a private session when that is necessary, as we did today and as we do regularly. Thank you. Ms. Susan Somers, I see you standing, to speed things up because we have some other things to address.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Judge. Ms. Mackintosh reminded me that I should raise or reraise the request I made yesterday about OTP presence in the video room, and I wanted to modify the request. I have studied carefully the Tadic decisions. Although there's nothing barring it, it does not necessarily address someone other than registry, although, again under Rule 90, there's -- with the videolink room being an extension of this courtroom, we would normally be able to have an investigator if it were someone -- if it were necessary. My concern is I need to be in communication with a staff member, and if the Chamber would be able to assist us, perhaps, in assuring us that a monitor is available to my staff member outside the room, and in moments of closed session, if that individual may have, perhaps, access only during those times, I think that would be for us quite satisfactory. We do not want to cause any concern to the registry about an established practice, and -- but it is quite important for us to have communication and that, unfortunately, I'm relegated to a fairly rough telephone system. And again, I would like to phrase this so that the Chamber realises we're not trying to ask for something exceptional, but just access as we need it. I have also indicated, Your Honour, that should the Defence have a similar request, we would not have opposed it under these circumstances for both parties to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not understanding. It may be late in the day. What -- the monitor that you want, what function? I don't understand what function the monitor -- you mean a monitor here in The Hague but outside of this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You want a monitor outside of where the actual testimony is being given?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We always, we always monitor open testimony, and there are communications -- as you know, we have equipment here where we're communicating constantly with our own persons on staff. And because of the physical difficulties of the communication, we would like to be able to make sure that our person representing us down there is able to follow the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Still, I don't want to take up time and I won't --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- but I don't understand. I mean, you're -- I've done -- I've seen video in a different case. And you're here, the person who's testifying is someplace with a representative of the registrar someplace else, you ask a question, and that person answers it just as if he or she were actually here. So I guess I'm thick, but I don't understand what purpose somebody outside a room away from where the person is testifying in Banja Luka or wherever it is, what function that person performs by having access to seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If there are questions that need quick clarification or if we need assistance on the ground for cross-examination, that individual is familiar with the issues, is watching the testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Couldn't that person be right here sitting behind you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, not likely because it would be on the ground in Banja Luka where we would need the assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And that person can't come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But we'd need the assistance in Banja Luka, and that person, we have someone going to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That person would run and get a document someplace in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I mean, I'm just talking --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment for the Judges to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, we will deal with several motions. Regarding this exception to have someone over there, the Chamber doesn't accept that exception. The Chamber orders that the video conference should be done normally, as it is normally done, which means everything is happening as if the witness were here in the courtroom. The parties and the Judges are here, and a representative of the registry will be there on the spot where the witness is with him. So no other persons will be present. So that is the decision of the Chamber: only the witness, the legal officer, and staff of the registry. Regarding the video conference for Mr. Prcac, in view of the motion of the Defence and having heard the parties yesterday and today in the courtroom, and noting that the motion was submitted by the Defence because the witness, due to reasons of health and the safety of his family, he does not wish to leave his country; in view of the fact that the Chamber does not consider a medical certificate to be necessary for a witness to be able to testify by video conference; and in view of the fact that the interests of justice will be served if this witness's testimony is heard by video conference, the Chamber grants the motion and states that also with respect to this witness, only the witness, the presiding officer, and, if necessary, a technician of the registry will be present in the video conference room. With respect to the question of translation, you know well what the question is so I'm not going to waste any time with that. I'm just going to tell you that the Chamber has consulted the translation service of the Tribunal, and they have confirmed that two different terms were used and that therefore there is no incoherence in the responses of the witness Delic. He testified that there were sef smjene in the police, shift leaders, but that there were no razvodnik straze. The translation service has provided us also with abstracts from dictionaries defining the term "razvodnik straze" which will be distributed to the parties. I think they have already been distributed to the parties. And therefore we see that this is a military term, as Mr. Fila alleged. The translation service also confirmed that the customary term that they use to translate shift leader is "sef smjene," and that the term "razvodnik straze" was used for the first time during the testimony of Mr. Delic. Therefore, the Chamber considers the matter settled and orders the admission into evidence of the memo of the translation service with its attachments, and to do that, I should like to ask Madam Registrar to give us a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this document, document C1, which means the first document of the Chamber, so you already have copies. The matter has been cleared up, and the Chamber will decide and weigh the probative value of all this at the end. So I think that the question of protective measures for Defence witnesses for Mr. Zigic have already been -- has already been decided as we have ruled, and I think there are no other matters to address. I see Mr. Jovan Simic, and I shall also give the floor to Ms. Susan Somers, saying that we really do have time constraints. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a short question. The decision as to videolink, does it apply to the videolinks to the Zigic defence on the 18th and 19th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I consulted the registrar previously, and the registrar said that there was no problem there and that your witness will be the witness following on from the Zigic witnesses. But let me just ask Madam Registrar to confirm that for the record. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it would be okay for the Prcac Defence to have one person testify through videolink. And this will be on the 17th and the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Ms. Susan Somers on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will take just a second, Your Honour, I need to clarify, let the Chamber know that yesterday we filed a response to the Banovic and Savic proposals for videolink by the Radic Defence without knowing that the Chamber had already ruled. We were never served with the Chamber's decision. I've spoken to the Registry about it and, please -- we are not withdrawing it, but please understand that we weren't -- we didn't mean to be out of order. We simply weren't informed that there was a decision rendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We never received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We took a decision on that. I think that Madam Registrar will see to that with you. Mr. Deretic, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, the Defence of Mr. Zigic, a long time ago, once suggested that for the Defence in this case, we would truly need -- it would be a great help if the Trial Chamber were able to, on the spot, to have an investigation and visit the site, and to have the Trial Chamber visit the investigation centres of both Keraterm and Omarska on the spot, on site. And I'm just saying -- bringing this up. And I personally, as a man from Prijedor, coming from Prijedor myself, I do consider that it would be indispensable for the Court, and of course for the Prosecution, to see for themselves on the spot, and to see that it is not as -- at all as black as it once was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, no, no. Once again, this is not the moment for allegations, Mr. Deretic. Now, if you want to give serious thought to that, perhaps you could do -- see about it with the Prosecution and send us a memorandum. But I think that the Chamber would be disposed only if it is necessary, because you know that we have a very heavy schedule. And having said that, we are always happy to receive memos from parties on issues of this kind. Let me say at the outset that it would be a little difficult to envisage this because of the heavy schedule, but I don't want to -- and the reasons why -- which this displacement would merit. And therefore -- the Chamber would like to understand things better, the entirety of the case. We are always at the parties' disposal, but we are not a tourist agency. We are here to work, to do our work. So only if it is absolutely necessary would we consider the fact. Let me say that we have a lot of work ahead of us today and that we will end there. I would like to wish everybody a happy Easter, for those of you who observe Easter. For others, a good weekend, good holiday, and every success in your work generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
